passage:
First week of March: at the sales review, Rashmi asked the regional head why customers were being told the loan offer had "no hidden charges" when the processing fee was in the fine print. The room went quiet. Maria, sitting beside her, looked at her notebook.
Two weeks later: the monthly awards were announced. Top performer went to the man who closed the most loans, no questions asked. Rashmi had been moved off the big corporate accounts "for fresh perspective." Everyone understood.
End of April: in a team huddle, a trainee asked Maria, quietly, if the fee line was really okay. Maria felt her throat tighten. She thought of her rent, her younger brother's college fees, the team that had welcomed her. "Just follow the script," she said. That night, she lay awake a long time, the trainee's face in her head.

qa.q: What was Rashmi moved off, and for what stated reason?
qa.a: Rashmi had been moved off the big corporate accounts for fresh perspective.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when the trainee asked about the fee line?
qa.a: Maria felt anxious and torn, afraid for her job and her family's needs and loyal to her team, yet uneasy enough to lie awake afterwards.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Maria at this stage?
qa.a: Maria could note down what she has seen and talk to someone she trusts outside the sales chain, such as the compliance team, instead of repeating follow the script.

qa.q: How might the trainee feel after Maria's answer?
qa.a: The trainee may feel confused and let down, learning from someone they trusted that questions are not welcome here.

grounding: Shows managers rewarding results without questions and sidelining a colleague who raised a concern, while fear and team loyalty silence someone still uneasy.

passage: "Sit, Chetan. You asked why I always ask about a company's targets before anything else. When I was twenty-five, a young woman at a pharmaceutical distributor in Chennai, I started to notice things. The targets doubled one year, and nobody could explain how we would reach them honestly. The one colleague who kept asking, a quiet man named Sampath, was moved to the stores. At lunch, people joked, 'Don't be a Sampath, don't ask too much.' When a shipment came back from a hospital, the manager said, 'Bring me good news only.' I laughed at the jokes too, at first. Then one evening I sat alone in the canteen, counted those signs on a paper napkin, and felt cold. Three signs in one year. That napkin is why I left before the audit came. Your Rukmini Amma is telling you, Chetan: watch the jokes. They tell you what people are afraid to say."

qa.q: Where was Sampath moved?
qa.a: Sampath was moved to the stores.

qa.q: What did Rukmini feel when she counted the signs on the napkin?
qa.a: Rukmini felt cold with alarm, suddenly seeing that the jokes and targets she had laughed along with were warning signs.

qa.q: In the story, which choice changed things, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sitting alone and writing the signs on a napkin let Rukmini see the pattern clearly, which is why she left before the audit came.

qa.q: How might Sampath have experienced those jokes at lunch?
qa.a: Sampath was probably hurt and isolated, hearing his honesty turned into a warning to others while he sat in the stores.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing the signs of organisational drift: honest people sidelined, impossible targets, fear of bad news and jokes about asking questions.

passage: Tariq had worked in quality at the sandwich factory outside Manchester for two years, long enough to know the allergen checks had become a quick glance. On Tuesday the call came: a boy had been taken to hospital after eating one of their egg sandwiches. It had contained sesame, not listed on the label. The supermarket had already pulled the whole batch from its shelves by noon. Tariq sat in the break room with the checklists in front of him, every box ticked in his own handwriting. His face burned. Clara, the site manager, came in and shut the door. "We'll say the label printer had a fault," she said. "No need to go into the checks." Tariq opened his mouth, then closed it. He thought of the boy, and then of his own signature. He nodded, and hated himself a little for it.

qa.q: By when had the supermarket pulled the batch from its shelves?
qa.a: The supermarket had already pulled the whole batch from its shelves by noon.

qa.q: What does Tariq's burning face suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Tariq feels deep shame, seeing his own handwriting on checks that were never really done after a boy was hurt.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Tariq after he nods?
qa.a: Tariq could go back to Clara or to the company's safety and compliance team the same day and tell the truth about the checks, so the real cause is fixed.

qa.q: How might the boy's family be affected if the printer story is accepted?
qa.a: The family would never learn the real cause, and other families could face the same risk if the checks stay broken.

grounding: Shows a customer being hurt so the cost of earlier shortcuts becomes visible, with sudden shame and pressure to cover up rather than admit it.

passage: I'm Rukmini from the accounts floor, and I saw most of what happened after the review. The outside auditors found that sales had been booked early for two years. Everyone expected the usual: a junior blamed, a memo, silence. Instead, at the all-staff meeting, Varun, our director, stood up and said, "This happened under me. I set targets that rewarded it." He named no juniors. He did name Keerthi from the finance desk, who had flagged the issue a year earlier, and said she would lead the fix, with a promise that no one would be penalised for raising it. I watched people's shoulders drop around the room. The next month, bonuses were tied to accurate forecasts, not just big numbers. I can't say what Varun felt. He looked tired. But people started bringing him bad news again.

qa.q: Who had flagged the issue a year earlier?
qa.a: Keerthi from the finance desk had flagged the issue a year earlier.

qa.q: How did people in the room seem to feel when Varun took responsibility?
qa.a: People seemed relieved, their shoulders dropping, because they no longer feared a junior being blamed.

qa.q: Which choices by Varun helped rebuild trust?
qa.a: He owned the problem publicly, protected and credited Keerthi who raised it, and changed bonuses to reward accurate forecasts instead of big numbers.

qa.q: What would change for Keerthi if Varun had blamed juniors instead?
qa.a: Keerthi would likely have felt unsafe and unheard, and people would have learned that raising issues is dangerous.

grounding: Shows an external review exposing a pattern, and a leader who owns it, protects the person who raised it and fixes the incentives, rebuilding trust.

passage:
[Friday, 6:15 pm]
Keerthana: Vijay, did you see the email about the new reporting line?
Vijay: Yes. Anonymous, goes straight to the outside ethics firm. Finally
Keerthana: And that "good catch" award for whoever flags a problem early 👏
Vijay: I nearly laughed. Two years ago you'd get moved to the basement for that
Keerthana: I'm still going to write my list though
Vijay: What list?
Keerthana: The one the trainer suggested. Three things I won't do, whatever the target. Written before I'm under pressure
Vijay: Okay what's on yours
Keerthana: 1. Sign for a check I didn't see. 2. Change a date on anything. 3. Tell a customer something I know is false
Vijay: Good one. Mine would add: notice when I start saying "it's just this once"
Keerthana: That's the sneaky one 😅
Vijay: Yeah. I said it three times last quarter
Keerthana: Then that's your line 🙂

qa.q: What are the three things on Keerthana's list?
qa.a: Sign for a check I didn't see, change a date on anything, and tell a customer something I know is false.

qa.q: How does Vijay seem to feel about the new reporting line?
qa.a: Vijay feels relieved and a bit amazed, remembering that two years ago people who flagged problems were punished.

qa.q: Why is writing the list before pressure a wise step?
qa.a: Deciding the lines in advance means Keerthana and Vijay can recognise a bend when it comes, instead of explaining it away in the moment.

qa.q: What might it be like for Vijay to admit saying it's just this once three times?
qa.a: Vijay may feel a little embarrassed but also honest and lighter, because naming it with a friend makes it easier to catch next time.

grounding: Shows an organisation creating a safe reporting line and rewarding early bad news, while individuals set their lines in advance and watch for explaining away discomfort.

passage:
Tanvir's diary, Wednesday night
Third day at the logistics firm. At four, Naveen, my senior, slid a delivery form across the desk and said, "Just put last Friday's date. The client needs it to show on time." My heart was pounding. Everyone was watching, or it felt like it. I said, "I can't put a date that isn't true. But I can write today's date and add a note saying the shipment was delayed by the port strike, with the port notice attached." Naveen stared at me for a second. Then he sighed and said, "Fine, try it. If the client shouts, you handle it." The client didn't shout. They just said thanks for the explanation.
I'm writing this down so I remember how it felt. Scary, but only for about a minute. If I'd said yes today, I think saying no next month would have been much harder.

qa.q: What did Naveen ask Tanvir to put on the form?
qa.a: Naveen asked Tanvir to put last Friday's date.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when Naveen slid the form across?
qa.a: Tanvir felt nervous, with a pounding heart and the sense that everyone was watching, but was determined to stay honest.

qa.q: Which of Tanvir's choices made refusing work?
qa.a: Tanvir said the reason simply and offered a true alternative, today's date with a delay note and the port notice, so the client still got what they needed.

qa.q: How might Naveen see the new hire after the client's reply?
qa.a: Naveen may feel surprised and perhaps a little respectful, seeing the honest way worked without trouble.

grounding: Shows a new hire declining to backdate a form, giving the reason simply and offering an honest alternative at the first bend.

passage:
Mentoring note by Irawati, programme mentor, after Thursday's session
Usha, six months into her role in the foundation's finance team, came to our session quieter than usual. She said she had been matching invoices and found payments for three training workshops in villages near Nashik that, as far as she could tell, never happened. No attendance sheets, no photos, and the hall owner's number did not work.
She kept saying, "There's probably an explanation." Maybe the sheets were filed elsewhere. Maybe her manager already knew. She also said, twice, "Someone senior must be handling it." She rubbed her neck the whole time.
What I did next: I told her it was natural to hope for an innocent reason. I suggested she write down exactly what she had seen, with dates and invoice numbers, and keep it safe, before deciding anything. We will meet again next Thursday.

qa.q: How many training workshops did Usha find payments for?
qa.a: She found payments for three training workshops that never happened as far as she could tell.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she talked and rubbed her neck?
qa.a: Usha felt a knot of unease and worry, and she was hoping an innocent explanation or someone senior would take the problem away.

qa.q: What was the mentor's suggestion, and why is it a sensible first step?
qa.a: The mentor suggested writing down exactly what Usha had seen, with dates and invoice numbers, so she has clear facts before deciding anything.

qa.q: How might the villagers who were meant to get the training be affected if nothing is done?
qa.a: They lose training that was paid for in their name, while the money goes somewhere else.

grounding: Shows an employee spotting a likely misuse of funds, feeling uneasy, and at first seeking innocent explanations and hoping someone else will handle it.

passage: "Himani, come, sit with your old Rafiq Chacha. You asked what I did at the cement plant when I was your age. I was twenty-six, a junior engineer. I noticed the stack emission readings in the report were always the same, day after day. Too neat. My first thought was, I'm new, I'm misunderstanding something. So I didn't run to anyone. For two months I kept my own notebook. I checked the raw sensor logs at night. I asked the senior technician, casually, how the readings were entered. He said, 'We copy the good day.' Even then I thought of my colleagues, good men with families, and of the people in the village downwind, coughing every winter. I went round and round. I only decided to act when I was sure, with the logs in my own hand, and that same year the filters were fixed. Remember that part, beti. Be sure first."

qa.q: How long did Rafiq keep his own notebook?
qa.a: He kept his own notebook for two months.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling as he went round and round?
qa.a: Rafiq felt torn and doubtful, loyal to colleagues with families but worried about the village people coughing downwind.

qa.q: In the story, which choice made Rafiq's later action stronger?
qa.a: Quietly checking the raw sensor logs and keeping his own notebook until he was sure meant he acted on facts, not suspicion.

qa.q: How might the people in the village downwind have been affected by the copied readings?
qa.a: They were breathing whatever the plant released while the reports showed a good day, so their coughing every winter was going unexplained.

grounding: Shows a person quietly gathering facts, questioning whether they misunderstand and weighing loyalty to colleagues against people who may be harmed before acting.

passage:
Sunday: Chetan sat on the balcony at 2 am with the printed emails in a folder, the proof that his company had been overstating its sales to the bank that lent it money. Mahima found him there. "Again?" He nodded. He couldn't stop picturing the HR office, the security guard taking his badge.
Wednesday: at lunch, he quietly asked his closest colleague whether he'd noticed anything odd in the quarter-end figures. The colleague looked away. "Don't drag me into this, Chetan." Chetan ate alone after that, feeling like the office had become glass.
The next Saturday: Mahima's mother asked about his promotion. Chetan smiled and changed the subject, thinking of the home loan and his daughter's school fees. That night Mahima said, "Whatever you decide, tell me first. We'll face it together." He held her hand tightly, too tired to answer, but for the first time in weeks he didn't feel completely alone.

qa.q: What time was Chetan sitting on the balcony on Sunday?
qa.a: Chetan sat on the balcony at 2 am.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling after his colleague looked away?
qa.a: Chetan felt alone and anxious, as if the whole office had become glass and no one would stand with him.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Chetan now that Mahima has spoken?
qa.a: Chetan can share the full picture with Mahima and, with her support, look into proper channels and qualified advice before deciding how to raise the false figures.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima to watch Chetan through these weeks?
qa.a: Mahima is worried and probably frightened too, but she chooses to stand with him and asks only to be told first.

grounding: Shows the fear of losing a job, family worries and isolation weighing on a would-be whistleblower, with lost sleep and few colleagues willing to speak.

passage: I'm Nitin, and I sit two desks from Pankaj at the hospital supplies company. Here is what I saw. For a week he stayed late, typing. On Monday he walked into our supervisor's cabin with a printed letter and came out ten minutes later. At lunch he told me, "I've put it in writing: the sterilisation records for batch 14 don't match the machine logs. I've copied the ethics office." He showed me his folder: a copy of the letter, the date and time he handed it over, and an email confirming receipt. The supervisor said it would be "looked into." The ethics office replied the same afternoon and asked for a meeting. The batch was put on hold that evening. I can't know if Pankaj was scared. His hands were steady, though, and he ate his whole lunch, which is more than I did.

qa.q: Which batch's sterilisation records did Pankaj say didn't match?
qa.a: Pankaj said the sterilisation records for batch 14 didn't match the machine logs.

qa.q: How does Pankaj seem to feel, going by Nitin's account?
qa.a: Pankaj seems calm and determined, with steady hands, though Nitin can't know whether Pankaj was also scared inside.

qa.q: Why was putting it in writing and keeping records a wise way to start?
qa.a: A written letter with dates and a confirmation creates a clear record, and it quickly showed who would act: the ethics office replied the same day and the batch was put on hold.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel watching Pankaj do this?
qa.a: Nitin seems nervous and perhaps admiring, since Nitin couldn't finish lunch while Pankaj stayed steady.

grounding: Shows an employee raising a concern in writing with a supervisor and the ethics office, keeping a record, and seeing who is willing to act.
